title: Dividing polynomials
objectives: Divide a polynomial by a linear factor, and use the factor theorem to factorise a cubic.

screens.prose: Take the cubic $f(x) = x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 6$. Fill in its value at each $x$; each value you type appears as a dot on the graph.
screens.question: Fill in $f(a)$ for each $a$.

hints.text: Substitute each value; keep negative numbers in brackets.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Substitute each value with care over the signs.

explain.text: Three values are 0: the curve crosses the axis at $x = 1$, 3 and $-2$. A product is zero when one bracket is zero (level 2), so $(x - 1)$, $(x - 3)$ and $(x + 2)$ should be factors. The value $f(2) = -4$ is not zero, so $(x - 2)$ should not be.

screens.prose: Slide $a$ along the whole numbers and watch $f(a)$ in the caption. Where $f(a) = 0$, the curve meets the axis.
screens.question: $f(3) = 0$. Which bracket should be a factor of $f(x)$?

options.why: $(x + 3)$ is zero at $x = -3$, and $f(-3) = -24$. A root at 3 needs a bracket that is zero at 3.

hints.text: A bracket that is zero at $x = 3$ makes the product zero there.

feedback.correct: $(x - 3)$ is zero at $x = 3$, where $f$ is zero.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which bracket is 0 when $x = 3$?

explain.text: $(x - 3)$ is 0 exactly when $x = 3$, which is where $f(3) = 0$. In the same way $f(1) = 0$ points to $(x - 1)$ and $f(-2) = 0$ to $(x + 2)$. The sign flips: a root at $a$ means the factor $(x - a)$.

screens.prose: Division runs the grid of level 1 backwards. Above, $252 \div 12$: the cells add to 252 and the rows are $10 + 2$. Below, $f(x) \div (x - 1)$: the cells add to $f(x)$. Each column head is one term of the answer.
screens.question: Read the column heads of the lower grid: $f(x) = (x - 1)(ax^2 + bx + c)$. Fill in $a$, $b$ and $c$.

hints.text: The top row is $x$ times each head: $x \times ? = x^3$.

feedback.correct: The heads are $x^2$, $-x$ and $-6$: the quotient is $x^2 - x - 6$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide each top-row cell by $x$ to get its column head.

byKey.sign-b: $x \times b = -x^2$ means $b = -1$. Check the bottom cell: $-1 \times (-x) = x$.
byKey.sign-c: $x \times c = -6x$ means $c = -6$. Check the bottom cell: $-1 \times (-6) = 6$.

explain.text: The heads are $x^2$, $-x$ and $-6$, as 20 and 1 were for $252 \div 12 = 21$. So $f(x) = (x - 1)(x^2 - x - 6) = (x - 1)(x - 3)(x + 2)$. The cells add up: $x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 6$.

screens.prose: **Factor theorem**: for a polynomial $f$, $(x - a)$ is a factor of $f(x)$ exactly when $f(a) = 0$, in both directions. **Remainder theorem**: dividing $f(x)$ by $(x - a)$ always leaves the remainder $f(a)$; a factor is the case where it is 0.
screens.question: What is the remainder when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x - 2)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The remainder on dividing by $(x - 2)$ is $f(2)$.

byKey.factor: A remainder of 0 would make $(x - 2)$ a factor, but $f(2) = -4$, not 0.

explain.text: By the remainder theorem the remainder is $f(2) = -4$. Indeed $f(x) = (x - 2)(x^2 - 5) - 4$: expand to check. Because the remainder is not 0, $(x - 2)$ is not a factor.

screens.prose: Divide $g(x) = 2x^3 + 3x^2 - 4x + 5$ by $(x + 2)$, one term at a time. $2x^3 \div x = 2x^2$, and $2x^2(x + 2) = 2x^3 + 4x^2$, which leaves $-x^2 - 4x + 5$ still to make. Carry on with $-x^2 \div x$, and write $g(x) = (x + 2)(ax^2 + bx + c) + r$.
screens.question: Fill in the quotient's coefficients and the remainder.

hints.text: After $2x^2$, what is left is $-x^2 - 4x + 5$. Divide its first term by $x$.
That leaves $3x^2 - 4x^2 = -x^2$, so the next term is $-x$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take one term at a time, subtracting what each term of the quotient accounts for.

explain.text: $(x + 2)(2x^2 - x - 2) = 2x^3 + 3x^2 - 4x - 4$, so 9 is left over to make $+5$. The remainder theorem agrees: $g(-2) = -16 + 12 + 8 + 5 = 9$. The point $(-2, 9)$ on the curve is that remainder.

screens.prose: Factorise $h(x) = x^3 - 7x + 6$ from scratch. A whole-number root $a$ must divide the constant 6, because $a^3 - 7a + 6 = 0$ gives $6 = a(7 - a^2)$, a multiple of $a$. So try $\pm 1$, $\pm 2$, $\pm 3$ and $\pm 6$. Note there is no $x^2$ term: its coefficient is 0.
screens.question: Factorise $h(x)$ fully.

hints.text: Roots 1, 2 and $-3$ give the factors $(x - 1)$, $(x - 2)$ and $(x + 3)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the three roots among the factors of 6, then write a bracket for each.

byKey.signs: Each bracket has the opposite sign to its root: the root $-3$ gives $(x + 3)$, the root 1 gives $(x - 1)$.
byKey.form: That is equal, but factorise fully: the quadratic factor still splits into two brackets.

explain.text: $h(1) = h(2) = h(-3) = 0$, so $h(x) = (x - 1)(x - 2)(x + 3)$; the leading coefficient 1 needs no number in front. Expand to check: $(x - 1)(x - 2) = x^2 - 3x + 2$, and times $(x + 3)$ gives $x^3 - 7x + 6$. Check the roots another way: $1 + 2 - 3 = 0$, which matches the missing $x^2$ term when the three brackets are expanded.

screens.prose: $(x - 2)$ is a factor of $p(x) = x^3 + kx^2 - 4$. Slide $k$ to see the curve change, then use the factor theorem.
screens.question: What is $k$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $p(2) = 0$ and solve for $k$.

byKey.no-constant: You left out the $-4$: $8 + 4k = 0$. The constant term stays: $8 + 4k - 4 = 0$.
byKey.minus-two: You used $p(-2) = 0$. The factor $(x - 2)$ means $x = 2$ is a root.

explain.text: $(x - 2)$ is a factor exactly when $p(2) = 0$, which is $8 + 4k - 4 = 0$, so $k = -1$. Then $p(x) = x^3 - x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x^2 + x + 2)$. At $k = -1$ the curve passes through $(2, 0)$.

screens.prose: A learner tests whether $(x + 3)$ is a factor of $h(x) = x^3 - 7x + 6$. They work out $h(3) = 27 - 21 + 6 = 12$ and say no.
screens.question: Is $(x + 3)$ a factor of $h(x)$?

options.why: You tested $x = 3$, as the learner did. $(x + 3)$ is zero at $x = -3$, so test $h(-3)$.
Whether 3 divides a coefficient is not the test. The test is the value $h(-3)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A bracket $(x + 3)$ is tested at the value that makes it zero.

byKey.wrong-test: You tested $h(3)$. The bracket $(x + 3)$ is zero at $x = -3$, and $h(-3) = 0$, so it is a factor.

explain.text: $(x + 3) = (x - (-3))$, so the factor theorem uses $a = -3$: $h(-3) = 0$, and it is a factor. $h(3) = 12$ is the remainder on dividing by $(x - 3)$, a different bracket. Write the bracket as $x - a$ first, then test $a$.

screens.prose: Factorise $k(x) = x^3 - 3x + 2$. $k(1) = 0$, and dividing by $(x - 1)$ gives $x^2 + x - 2$. Look at how the curve meets the axis at $x = 1$.
screens.question: Factorise $k(x)$ fully.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Factorise the quadratic factor too, and keep both copies of $(x - 1)$.

byKey.form: Factorise fully: $x^2 + x - 2$ still splits into $(x - 1)(x + 2)$.
byKey.signs: The roots are 1 and $-2$, so the brackets are $(x - 1)$ and $(x + 2)$.
byKey.lost-square: That is a quadratic, not $k(x)$. $(x - 1)$ appears twice: once from the division and once from $x^2 + x - 2$.

explain.text: $k(x) = (x - 1)(x^2 + x - 2) = (x - 1)^2(x + 2)$. A squared factor makes a repeated root: the curve touches the axis at $x = 1$ without crossing. At $x = -2$ it crosses.

screens.prose: Why does dividing $f(x)$ by $(x - a)$ leave $f(a)$? Division by $(x - a)$ gives a quotient $q(x)$ and a remainder $r$, a number, because it has a lower degree than $x - a$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the proof in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: $f(x) = (x - a)q(x) + r$ for every $x$: this is what the division means
$f(a) = (a - a)q(a) + r$: put $x = a$ into the identity
So $(x - a)$ is a factor exactly when $r = 0$, that is, when $f(a) = 0$
$f(-a) = (-a - a)q(-a) + r$: put $x = -a$ into the identity
lines.why: Putting $x = -a$ leaves $-2a\,q(-a)$, which is not zero. Choose the $x$ that makes $x - a$ zero: $x = a$.

hints.text: Start from what the division gives.
Then choose the $x$ that makes the bracket $(x - a)$ zero.

feedback.correct: With $x = a$ the bracket vanishes, so $f(a) = r$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the division as an identity, then put $x = a$.

byKey.d4: The factor statement comes last, after $f(a) = r$ is shown.

explain.text: The identity $f(x) = (x - a)q(x) + r$ holds for every $x$, so it holds at $x = a$. There the bracket is 0, leaving $f(a) = r$. A zero remainder means $(x - a)$ divides exactly: the factor theorem in both directions.

screens.prose: You invest £1,000 and receive £400, £480 and £576 after years 1, 2 and 3. Grown at a factor $x$ a year to the end of year 3, the cost is $1000x^3$ and the receipts are $400x^2 + 480x + 576$. They match when $1000x^3 - 400x^2 - 480x - 576 = 0$. $x = 1.2$ is a root (20% a year), and the cubic factorises as $8(5x - 6)(25x^2 + 20x + 12)$.
screens.question: What is the discriminant of $25x^2 + 20x + 12$?

feedback.correct: $400 - 1200 = -800 < 0$: the quadratic factor has no real root.

byKey.plus: You added $4ac$. The discriminant subtracts it: $400 - 1200$.
byKey.sign: You worked out $4ac - b^2$. The discriminant is $b^2 - 4ac = 400 - 1200 = -800$.

explain.text: $b^2 - 4ac = 400 - 1200 = -800$, which is negative, so $25x^2 + 20x + 12$ has no real root. The only real rate is $x = 1.2$, a 20% yearly return. Check: $1000 \times 1.728 = 1728$ and $400 \times 1.44 + 480 \times 1.2 + 576 = 1728$.

ideas: Division runs the grid backwards: $f(x) = (x - a)q(x) + r$, one term of the quotient at a time, with a column for every missing power.
Factor theorem: $(x - a)$ is a factor of a polynomial $f(x)$ exactly when $f(a) = 0$; remainder theorem: $f(a)$ is always the remainder.
To factorise a cubic with whole-number coefficients and leading coefficient 1, try the factors of the constant; a negative discriminant in the quadratic factor means one real root.

formula.name: Remainder theorem
formula.note: So $(x - a)$ is a factor if and only if $f(a) = 0$.

summary.trap: Dividing by $(x + 2)$ tests $f(-2)$, not $f(2)$: write the bracket as $x - a$ first.

options.why: You left no column for $0x^2$ and divided $x^2 - 7x + 6$ instead. Write $x^3 + 0x^2 - 7x + 6$.
That times $(x - 1)$ gives $x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 6$. Here the $x^2$ term is 0, so the quotient has $+x$.
$-1 \times 6 = -6$, not $+6$: the quotient's constant must be $-6$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $x^3 + 0x^2 - 7x + 6$ and divide one term at a time.

explain.text: With the column $0x^2$ in place: $x^2(x - 1) = x^3 - x^2$ leaves $x^2$, so the next term is $+x$. Then $x(x - 1) = x^2 - x$ leaves $-6x + 6 = -6(x - 1)$. The quotient is $x^2 + x - 6$.

quiz.question: How many real roots does $x^3 + x - 2 = 0$ have?

options.why: A cubic can have three, but $x^2 + x + 2$ has discriminant $1 - 8 = -7$: no real roots.
A cubic has exactly two different real roots only when one is repeated, as in $(x - 1)^2(x + 2)$. Here the quadratic factor has discriminant $-7$, so it adds none.

feedback.correct: Only $x = 1$: the quadratic factor has discriminant $-7$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the discriminant of the quadratic factor.

explain.text: $x - 1 = 0$ gives $x = 1$. The factor $x^2 + x + 2$ has discriminant $1 - 4 \times 2 = -7 < 0$, so no real roots. One real root in all.

quiz.question: What is the remainder when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x + 1)$?

options.why: $-4$ is the constant term, the remainder on dividing by $x$. Here use $f(-1)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the remainder theorem with $a = -1$.

explain.text: $(x + 1) = (x - (-1))$, so the remainder is $f(-1) = 2(-1) - 1 + 3(-1) - 4 = -10$. Note $f(1) = 0$, so $(x - 1)$ is a factor, but $(x + 1)$ is not.

options.why: You took $3x^2$ as 6 instead of 12 at $x = 2$. $3 \times 2^2 = 12$, so $f(2) = 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the factor theorem with $a = 2$.

explain.text: $f(2) = 8 - 12 + 4 = 0$, so $(x - 2)$ is a factor. In fact $f(x) = (x - 2)^2(x + 1)$, a repeated factor. The curve touches the axis at 2 and crosses at $-1$.
